title: Plan to End H-1B Grace Period Draws 31,383 Public Comments Before Deadline
excerpt: The DHS proposal to delete the 60-day window after a job loss is still only a proposal — the grace period remains in effect while the department reviews the record.
body:
• A Department of Homeland Security proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period after a job loss drew 31,383 posted public comments by Tuesday night, up from about 27,000 on November 2.
  • The proposal is not law: the grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) remains in effect today for H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN and other workers and their dependents.
  • Comments closed on November 10. DHS must review the submissions before it can publish a final rule, and only a final rule would set an effective date.
  • About 70% of the 406,348 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal 2025 were for workers born in India, according to USCIS figures cited in coverage of the rule.

A Trump administration proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period that lets laid-off foreign workers stay in the United States while they find a new job drew more than 31,000 public comments before the deadline, according to IANS reporting from Washington. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had received 31,383 posted comments by Tuesday night, a count that rose from about 27,000 on November 2 to 30,382 early Tuesday as the submission window closed.

Who is affected, exactly

The proposal covers workers whose US status is tied to a job that has ended: H-1B and H-1B1 professionals, L-1 intracompany transferees, O-1 workers, E-1, E-2 and E-3 treaty workers and TN professionals, together with their dependents. It does not change anything for workers who are still employed, and it does not touch the separate F-1 student grace period. Because roughly 70% of approved H-1B petitions in fiscal 2025 went to India-born workers, according to the USCIS report to Congress cited in coverage, Indian professionals would carry most of the impact if the rule is finalised.

What would change

Under the current regulation, 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), a worker whose employment ends may remain for up to 60 days, or until their authorised stay expires, whichever is shorter. In that window they can start with a new employer that files a petition, change to a different status, or prepare to leave the country. The provision has been in place since a 2016 regulation took effect on January 17, 2017.

The proposed rule, published on September 11 at 91 FR 57807 under docket USCIS-2026-0364, would delete that provision. DHS argues the grace period "is not mandated by statute," that immigration status should stay tied to the specific employment for which a worker was admitted, and that the current rule creates administrative work: the department said adjudicators had to review grace-period eligibility across more than 1.9 million petitions and applications between October 2017 and May 2026. The comment count alone does not show how many submissions support or oppose the change, as IANS noted in its report.

What to do next

Nothing changes today. A worker laid off this week still has the grace period, because a proposed rule has no legal effect until DHS publishes a final rule with its own effective date. The practical steps for affected readers are unchanged: count the 60 days from the last day of employment, use the window to secure a new sponsor's petition or a change of status, and keep the deadline in view rather than the comment headlines. What to watch next is the Federal Register: after reviewing the comments, DHS will either publish a final rule specifying when the change takes effect, amend the proposal, or let it lapse.

The grace-period docket was one of three DHS proposals with comment deadlines in the same week, alongside a proposed OPT fee rule and a proposal to end USCIS deference to its own earlier approvals, according to a deadline tracker published on November 2. Of the roughly 32,400 comments filed across the three dockets by November 2, about 84% went to the grace-period proposal.
